newsitem.title: USA: Fierce rivalry seen as Mexican phone market opens up.
newsitem.headline: Fierce rivalry seen as Mexican phone market opens up.

text.p: The opening of the Mexican long-distance telephone market Jan. 1 will spark a fierce struggle among big phone companies for a slice of the pie even as it doubles in size, industry executives said.
Watch out for a Chilean-style shakeout of telephone companies, the executives told a Bear Stearns Investors Conference Wednesday.
Chile has seen seven or eight long-distance carriers cut to three in the two years of competition, with the rest relegated to marginal roles.

"If everybody built everything they told the (Mexican) government they would build, we would have railroad tracks of fiber (optic cables) ... enough to serve the entire western hemisphere," said Robert Lacy director of regulatory and legal affairs for Avantel, a joint venture between MCI Communications Corp. and Mexico's Grupo Financiero Banamex Accival SA de CV.
"I don't see there being a fifth, sixth or seventh national network. There are only three in the United States," he said.

Jorge Escalona, chief executive of Alestra, a joint venture between AT&T Corp. and Mexico's Bancomer, predicted Telefonos de Mexico SA or Telmex, now the main long-distance provider, could see its market share halved by 2000.
"By the year 2000, I would expect Mexico will be a very competitive market place in telephony in all markets and categories," he said.
On Jan. 1, the long-distance networks can begin connecting their systems to Telmex local lines, greatly speeding long-distance competition.
Bell Atlantic Corp.'s Grupo Iusacell SA has about 2-1/2 percent of the long-distance market now as Telmex's sole competitor.
However, Adolfo Cerezo, Telmex chief financial officier, said that based on the opening of other telephone markets Telmex could see its market share fall 30 percent over the next few years.
William Kingman, chief financial officer of Iusacell said the long-distance market probably would double to $9 billion a year by 2000.

Executives criticised Telmex for allegedly subsidising local and other services with revenues from its more lucrative long-distance lines. Telephone companies have invested well over $1 billion in preparation for the opening of the long-distance market.
The other companies contended the subsidies gave Telmex an unfair advantage. Such subsidies for local service are barred as of Jan. 1.
